newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Rivals deplore state loan plan for Kirch.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rivals deplore state loan plan for Kirch.

text.p: Bavaria's government offered local media tycoon Leo Kirch a helping hand on Monday in the shape of a massive credit line, provoking a stream of protests from the media industry and opposition politicians.

Kirch, whose ambitions to establish himself as Germany's king of digital television have been thwarted by weak sales and legal disputes, is in talks to receive a partly state-sponsored loan of several hundred million marks, possibly as big as one billion marks ($591 million).
Coming just weeks after British Sky Broadcasting Plc (BSkyB) abandoned plans to invest in his DF1 digital station, the loan should give Kirch valuable breathing space.

But the IG Medien trade union, top media figures and politicians accused Bavarian authorities of subsidising the Kirch group in its aim to monopolise German digital pay television, which is still in its infant stages.

"A regional government, which is supposed to stand for market forces, is supporting a big business which is aiming for a monopoly and therefore ruining prices for us as well," Jobst Plog, director of the Hamburg-based media group Norddeutscher Rundfunk, said in a radio interview.
"We have to wonder what it means for competition if the state has to help someone build up the digital TV business they failed to build up alone," said a spokeswoman for rival pay TV group Premiere.

Already the owner of Europe's biggest film library, Kirch's efforts -- at an estimated cost of 10 billion marks -- to secure blockbuster programmes have vastly inflated German prices for rights to big-ticket items, angering his peers.

Kirch itself declined comment, except to confirm that the talks were taking place. It was therefore unclear what the scale of the loan being negotiated was or what the money would be used for, although sources said Kirch would invest the funds in films.

Landesanstalt fuer Aufbaufinanzierung (LfA), the bank controlled by the Bavarian state government which alone is to provide Kirch with "several hundred million marks" in credit, denied that it was organising state aid for Kirch.
The bank said several commercial banks were also involved, and that the business would be arranged according to regular market principles.

The news comes amid mounting signs that Kirch's digital TV plans have gone awry. His DF1 service has attracted fewer than 30,000 customers in its starting months and Kirch has been forced back into talks on possible co-operation with rival Bertelsmann AG.

Premiere, which is Germany's only analogue pay TV channel and is controlled by Bertelsmann AG and Canal Plus of France, said it was still negotiating a possible link-up between its customer base and the DF1 digital platform.
Weak sales forced Kirch back into talks with Bertelsmann and Canal Plus after he parted company with them in a highly publicised squabble over decoder standards last July.
"We are still fundamentally in favour of links. Which is not to say we cannot survive without such an agreement," Premiere's spokeswoman said.

With some 1.5 million subscribers, Premiere has been able to launch its own pilot digital TV project with around 30,000 subscribers and believes thousands more would be willing to trade their analogue services for digital services.

Digital technology allows broadcasters to squeeze more channels into cable and satellite networks and show films in very high quality. It also allows new media forms such as video on demand and home-shopping.
A deal with Premiere would also ease Kirch's legal troubles. Premiere has mounted a series of legal challenges on Kirch, successfully curtailing advertising for DF1.
He still owns 25 percent of Premiere and is its main supplier of films.

Kirch is also thought to be close to a deal with Deutsche Telekom AG, which has so far refused to endorse Kirch's decoder technology and excluded DF1 from its cable TV network that links 16.7 million homes. ($ = 1.691 German Marks)
